correctness.rationale: If c,d,e count selected length-three words with one, two, and three distinct ordered shadows, only constants contribute to c and every word counted in c or d hits a diagonal. This is immediate by comparing (a,b), (a,c), (b,c): with three distinct symbols all differ, while a nonconstant word with just two shadows must have an adjacent equal pair. Hence c≤q, c+d≤2q, and 3|C|=I+2c+d≤2q²+3q, yielding the floor bound for q≥2. In each Steiner block each of the two reversal pairs gives every ordered off-diagonal pair once, and the unique unordered-pair incidence prevents clashes across blocks. Replacing abc by aab, bbc, acc preserves ab, bc, ac and adds exactly one incidence to each of aa, bb, cc. Together with the constants, disjointness of the selected blocks makes every list of size at most two. The added words cannot coincide with any other block's added words since a distinct-symbol pair determines their block. The resulting size q+2q(q−1)/3+2m is optimal for m=q/3 if q≡3 mod 6 and m=(q−1)/3 if q≡1 mod 6. The first existence statement is classical Kirkman existence as confirmed in the Kirkman survey. For the latter, even without recovering the full newer citation, Vanstone et al.'s published abstract states Hanani systems exist at q≡1 mod 6 except q=7,13, and each has an almost parallel class by definition; at 13 the two explicit cyclic bases in the frozen checker independently give a Steiner system with four disjoint blocks. At 7 the separately listed 39 words are distinct, cover 47 outputs twice and two once, and attain the floor bound. Equality is not claimed at other q, nor for a different length, deletion budget or list size.

The problem naturally tests how directed off-diagonal coverage interacts with repeated symbols and is not an isolated alphabet computation.
